newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says Maastricht deficit goal achievable.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says Maastricht deficit goal achievable.

text.p: German unemployment may be slightly higher in 1997 than the government has forecast, but this will not prevent Bonn from reaching the deficit target required to join Europe's single currency, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday.

"Unemployment will be a bit higher than in the government's annual economic report," Waigel told reporters after a closed hearing of parliament's budget committee. The report in January forecast average unemployment at 4.1 million this year.
Germany's six leading economic institutes on Tuesday said they expected unemployment to average 4.28 million this year.

Commenting on a European Commission report earlier today showing that Germany's deficit would exactly meet the deficit target of 3.0 percent of gross domestic product this year, Waigel said: "Three-point-zero percent is achievable. That is correct. That is what I've always said."
Conceding that tax revenues in the first quarter were running below budgeted levels, Waigel said he could not give precise figures until official tax estimates for 1997 are released in mid-May.
But he said there were special factors which meant that the first quarter data were not a reliable indicator for the year as a whole.
Waigel said that he expected the 1997 tax estimates to be revised down by between eight and 10 billion marks, but rejected the institutes' view that the shortfall could be as big as 20 billion marks.

Such a big shortfall would make it difficult, but not impossible, to meet the single currency's borrowing target, the institutes said on Tuesday. They forecast a 1997 German budget deficit of between 3.0 and 3.2 percent of GDP.
